Designed to help owners better understand their cat and improve its quality of life.
Not always a sign of well-being — it can also signal stress.
Purring is produced by vibration of the larynx. It often signals well-being, but also self-soothing in cases of stress or pain.
Observe the overall context before concluding the cat is happy.
A sign of trust and affection from your cat.
The cat slowly narrows its eyes toward you as a sign of trust. Responding in kind strengthens the bond.
Mirror this signal to reinforce the relationship.
Staring at the cat without blinking — this can be perceived as a threat.
A vertical tail indicates friendly intent and confidence. A small hook at the tip signals a particularly warm greeting.
Respond positively to this invitation for contact.
A sign of agitation or irritation.
Unlike dogs, a cat flicking its tail is irritated or overexcited. It is not a sign of joy.
Stop interacting and let the cat calm down.
Continuing to pet or play with a cat whose tail is flicking.
When ears flatten back, the cat is frightened or ready to react aggressively. Stop all interaction immediately.
Continuing to touch or approach a cat with flattened ears.
A sign of trust, not necessarily an invitation.
Exposing the belly shows extreme trust, but is not always an invitation to be petted. Many cats scratch if this vulnerable area is touched.
Check whether the cat truly accepts belly petting before insisting.
Automatically petting a cat\'s belly when it rolls over.
A well-being behavior rooted in the nursing period.
The cat kneads with its front paws — a gesture inherited from kittens nursing their mother. A sign of comfort and security.
Let this behavior happen — it is a very good sign.
Punishing or abruptly interrupting this moment of well-being.
Affectionate marking and a sign of trust.
The cat rubs its muzzle, cheeks or temple to deposit pheromones. It is a sign of trust and affectionate bonding.
Respond positively to this cat-initiated contact.
Pushing away a cat that comes to rub its head.
A reaction to an unreachable prey.
This rapid sound is produced when the cat watches a bird or prey it cannot catch. An expression of frustration and activated hunting instinct.
Offer a play session with a feather wand to channel this instinct.
A vital need for marking and claw maintenance.
Cats scratch to mark territory (paw pad pheromones), stretch and maintain their claws. It is a fundamental need.
Provide varied scratching posts in the right places (near resting areas).
Punishing scratching — it does not eliminate the need; the cat will find other surfaces.
Territorial communication, often linked to stress.
The cat urinates while standing and backing up, tail trembling. This marking behavior is distinct from normal elimination. In a neutered cat, it often signals territorial stress.
Identify and reduce the source of stress (visible outdoor cat, conflict with a housemate).
Punishing the cat — this worsens stress and therefore marking.
Often linked to a lack of daytime stimulation.
Cats are naturally active at dawn and dusk. A lack of play during the day can result in nighttime agitation.
Offer an intense play session before bedtime, then a meal.
Letting the cat get bored all day and being surprised by its nighttime agitation.
Often linked to stress or boredom.
A cat that destroys things when alone is not acting out of revenge. It is a sign of distress or boredom.
Enrich the environment: rotating toys, accessible windows, hiding spots.
Punishing after the fact — the cat does not connect the punishment to its past behavior.
Several possible causes depending on context.
Excessive meowing can signal hunger, boredom, attention-seeking, pain, or in older cats, early cognitive syndrome. Siamese and oriental breeds are naturally more vocal.
Consult a vet if vocalizations are new, nocturnal and intense.
Systematically responding to vocal demands — this reinforces the behavior.
Some human foods can be dangerous for cats.

To be safe, avoid chocolate, onion, garlic, grapes, alcohol, cooked bones, and very fatty or salty foods. Cow\'s milk is also poorly tolerated by most adult cats. If ingestion is suspected and symptoms appear, consult a vet promptly.

Lilies (highly toxic, can cause kidney failure), philodendron, pothos, azalea, and lily of the valley are among the most dangerous plants. If your cat has chewed an unknown plant and shows symptoms, seek emergency veterinary care.
Cooked bones can splinter and cause internal injuries. Avoid them entirely. Raw bones may be offered under supervision, but ask your vet first.
In moderation and depending on the vegetable.

Some cooked vegetables such as carrot or zucchini may be tolerated in small amounts. A cat\'s diet must remain primarily meat-based — cats are strict carnivores and cannot synthesize certain essential amino acids such as taurine.
Useful for positive reinforcement, but keep them controlled.
Treats can be useful during play or training sessions. They should not exceed 10% of the daily ration. Choose treats designed for cats, with minimal additives.
How to change your cat\'s food?
Change the diet over 7 to 10 days by gradually mixing the old and new food. Cats are very sensitive to dietary changes and may suddenly refuse new food or develop digestive issues.
What if my cat ate something questionable?
Identify what the cat ingested and in what approximate quantity. Do not try to induce vomiting yourself. Contact your vet or the veterinary poison control center if the substance may be toxic.
Which signs should alert you after ingestion?
Some signs require urgent veterinary attention.
Repeated vomiting, severe diarrhea, lethargy, trembling, breathing difficulties, excessive drooling, convulsions or unusual behavior are warning signs. Consult without delay.
Why does my cat eat grass?
Grass helps cats eliminate hairballs and can act as a natural purgative. Offer cat grass or a pot of chewing grass — it is beneficial for most indoor cats.
My cat is vomiting — is it serious?
It depends on frequency and context.
An isolated hairball vomit is often benign. Frequent vomiting with blood, combined with lethargy or refusal to eat, requires veterinary consultation.
Hairballs: how to help your cat?
A common issue with simple solutions.
Brush your cat regularly, offer cat grass, and consider a specific anti-hairball diet. In cases of very frequent vomiting or constipation, consult a vet.
My cat always begs for food
Food-seeking behavior can have several causes.

A cat that frequently begs may lack stimulation, have an insufficient ration, or have developed a begging habit. Food puzzles (treat dispensers) can help channel this behavior while providing mental stimulation.
